subChunks.title: Console I/O with Scanner
subChunks.hookHtml: A spell that can't receive input from the outside world is useless. Java's Scanner class lets your programs read from the console, from strings, or from files — making them truly interactive.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Reading from the console

import java.util.Locale;
import java.util.Scanner;

Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in);
sc.useLocale(Locale.US); // fix: nextDouble() is locale-sensitive; US locale uses '.' not ','

System.out.print("Enter your name: ");
String name = sc.nextLine();  // reads a full line

System.out.print("Enter your age: ");
int age = sc.nextInt();       // reads an integer

System.out.print("Enter your score: ");
double score = sc.nextDouble(); // reads a decimal (expects '.' with Locale.US)

sc.close(); // always close the scanner when done

Locale note: nextDouble() uses the JVM's default locale to parse decimal numbers — European locales use a comma (1,5) not a dot (1.5). Always call sc.useLocale(Locale.US) immediately after constructing the Scanner to ensure consistent behaviour across all environments. Alternatively, read the value as a String with nextLine() and parse it with Double.parseDouble(), which always expects a dot.

Reading numbers safely

If the user types letters when an integer is expected, nextInt() throws InputMismatchException. Validate first with hasNextInt():

if (sc.hasNextInt()) {
    int n = sc.nextInt();
} else {
    System.out.println("Please enter a whole number.");
    sc.next(); // discard the invalid token
}

The nextLine() after nextInt() trap

After nextInt(), the newline character is left in the buffer. A subsequent nextLine() reads an empty string. Fix: add an extra sc.nextLine() call to consume the leftover newline:

int age = sc.nextInt();
sc.nextLine(); // consume leftover newline
String comment = sc.nextLine(); // now reads the actual next line

Reading from a String (useful for testing)

Scanner sc = new Scanner("42 3.14 hello");
int    n = sc.nextInt();
double d = sc.nextDouble();
String s = sc.next();
System.out.println(n + " " + d + " " + s); // 42 3.14 hello

storyBeats.text: A letter arrives from a distant kingdom asking for a spell that can listen as well as speak. Eldrin hands you an enchanted quill — the Academy's Scanner.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: All the programs you have written so far run the same way every time. Real software must respond to input. Java's Scanner class reads text from any source — the keyboard, a file, or a string — and parses it into whatever type you need.

storyBeats.speaker: Reading from the console
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: There is a subtle trap awaiting you. After reading an integer with nextInt(), the newline you pressed to confirm is still sitting in the buffer. Your next nextLine() will grab that empty line instead of the text you type. Consume the newline first with an extra sc.nextLine() call.

storyBeats.speaker: The nextLine() trap fix
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: In tests and practice, you can construct a Scanner from a String instead of System.in. This lets you simulate user input without typing. An invaluable trick for writing testable interactive programs.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
In this exercise, the test runner injects input automatically. Write a program that:

  1. Creates a Scanner reading from System.in.
  2. Reads a String for a wizard's name.
  3. Reads an int for their level.
  4. Reads a double for their mana reserve.
  5. Prints: "Wizard: [name], Level [level], Mana [mana]"

Test input will be: Lyria, 5, 88.5 (one per line).
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain how Java's Scanner works. What is the 'nextLine() after nextInt()' pitfall, and why does it happen? How would you explain it to a junior developer?
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
From a blank file, create an interactive quiz that accepts input from System.in. The test runner will inject the answers:

  • Print a question: "What is 7 * 6?" and read the answer as a String.
  • If the answer equals "42", print "Correct!". Otherwise print "Wrong. The answer is 42.".
  • Print a second question: "What type holds a single character in Java?" and read the answer.
  • If the trimmed, lowercase answer equals "char", print "Correct!". Otherwise print "Wrong. The answer is char.".
  • Count correct answers and print: "Score: [n]/2".

questions.questionHtml: Which Scanner method reads an entire line including spaces?
questions.explanationHtml: nextLine() reads everything up to (and consuming) the newline character. next() reads only the next token (stops at whitespace). readLine() is a method on BufferedReader, not Scanner.

questions.questionHtml: Why does a nextLine() call after nextInt() sometimes return an empty string?
options: Scanner has a bug in this combination
nextInt() consumes the number but leaves the newline in the buffer, which nextLine() immediately reads
nextLine() needs to be called twice to skip the int
The Scanner buffer is flushed after nextInt()
questions.correctAnswer: nextInt() consumes the number but leaves the newline in the buffer, which nextLine() immediately reads
questions.explanationHtml: nextInt() reads the integer token but stops before the newline character the user pressed. The newline remains in the input buffer. The next nextLine() reads everything up to that newline — which is nothing, giving an empty string. Fix: call sc.nextLine() once extra after nextInt() to consume the leftover newline.

questions.questionHtml: You can construct a Scanner from a String to simulate user input in tests.
questions.explanationHtml: new Scanner("42 hello 3.14") creates a Scanner that reads from that string. This is very useful for unit testing code that accepts Scanner input without requiring actual console interaction.

questions.questionHtml: What should you do if a user types letters when your code calls sc.nextInt()?
options: The program crashes and that is acceptable
Call hasNextInt() first; if false, consume the invalid token with next() and prompt again
Use nextLine() then Integer.parseInt() with a try/catch for NumberFormatException
questions.correctAnswer: Use nextLine() then Integer.parseInt() with a try/catch for NumberFormatException
questions.explanationHtml: The safest pattern for robust numeric input: read the whole line with nextLine(), then parse with Integer.parseInt() inside a try/catch for NumberFormatException. This avoids the buffer-leftover problem and gives you full control over the error message.

subChunks.title: File Reading & Writing
subChunks.hookHtml: Spell data that only lives in memory is lost when the program ends. Writing to and reading from files gives your programs persistence — the ability to save and load data between runs.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Writing a file

import java.io.FileWriter;
import java.io.PrintWriter;
import java.io.IOException;

try (PrintWriter pw = new PrintWriter(new FileWriter("spells.txt"))) {
    pw.println("Fireball");
    pw.println("Ice Lance");
    pw.printf("Heal (cost: %d mana)%n", 20);
} catch (IOException e) {
    System.err.println("Write failed: " + e.getMessage());
}
// PrintWriter is auto-closed by try-with-resources

To append instead of overwrite: new FileWriter("spells.txt", true) — the second argument enables append mode.

Reading a file — BufferedReader

import java.io.BufferedReader;
import java.io.FileReader;

try (BufferedReader br = new BufferedReader(new FileReader("spells.txt"))) {
    String line;
    while ((line = br.readLine()) != null) {
        System.out.println(line);
    }
} catch (IOException e) {
    System.err.println("Read failed: " + e.getMessage());
}

Modern alternative: Files utility (Java 11+)

import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.util.List;

// Write all lines at once
Files.writeString(Path.of("spells.txt"), "Fireball\nHeal\n");

// Read all lines into a List
List<String> lines = Files.readAllLines(Path.of("spells.txt"));
lines.forEach(System.out::println);

// Read entire file as one String
String content = Files.readString(Path.of("spells.txt"));

Paths and directories

import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.nio.file.Paths;

Path p = Path.of("data", "logs", "app.log"); // cross-platform
System.out.println(p.toAbsolutePath());

storyBeats.text: Your spellbook is filling up. You need to save your progress. Eldrin hands you a quill enchanted to write to any surface — parchment, stone, file system.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Memory is temporary. A file endures. Java's I/O classes let you write data to the file system and read it back. There are many layers — FileWriter at the bottom, PrintWriter adding convenience methods on top. Wrap them in try-with-resources and the file is always properly closed.

storyBeats.speaker: Writing a file
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Reading works in reverse: BufferedReader wraps FileReader and adds line-by-line reading. The pattern while ((line = br.readLine()) != null) is the classic Java idiom for reading until end-of-file.

storyBeats.speaker: Reading a file
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Modern Java's Files utility is even simpler. Files.readAllLines() gives you a List<String> in one call. Files.writeString() writes a whole string at once. For quick scripts and small files, this is the idiomatic approach.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Write a program that:

  1. Writes three lines to a file called "output.txt": "Line 1: Foundation", "Line 2: Advanced", "Line 3: Expert"
  2. Reads the file back and prints each line.
  3. Prints how many lines were read.

Use PrintWriter for writing and BufferedReader for reading, with try-with-resources for both.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain Java file I/O to a beginner. What are the key classes involved? What is the difference between the classic BufferedReader approach and the modern Files utility? Why must files always be closed?
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
From a blank file, implement a simple log system:

  • Define a method log(String filename, String message) that appends a line to the file: "[LOG] [message]". Use append mode (new FileWriter(filename, true)).
  • Call log three times with different messages: "Server started", "User logged in", "Spell cast: Fireball".
  • Read all lines from the file using Files.readAllLines() and print each.
  • Print the total number of log entries.

questions.questionHtml: Which Java class is commonly used to write formatted text to a file?
questions.explanationHtml: PrintWriter wraps FileWriter and provides println() and printf() methods, making it convenient for writing text. FileOutputStream writes raw bytes. FileReader and Scanner are for reading.

questions.questionHtml: How do you open a file for appending (adding to end) rather than overwriting?
questions.explanationHtml: new FileWriter(path, true) opens the file in append mode. The boolean true means 'append'. Default (false) truncates the file on open. Files.appendString() is not a real method (use Files.writeString(path, content, StandardOpenOption.APPEND)).

questions.questionHtml: Files.readAllLines() is suitable for reading very large files (several GB).
questions.explanationHtml: Files.readAllLines() loads the entire file into a List<String> in memory. For very large files, use Files.lines() which returns a lazy Stream<String>, or use BufferedReader to process one line at a time.

questions.questionHtml: A server processes millions of log lines per day. The log file can be 10+ GB. Which file-reading approach is most appropriate?
options: Files.readString() — reads everything into one String
BufferedReader + readLine() in a loop — processes one line at a time without loading the whole file
Scanner with nextLine() — flexible and easy to use
questions.correctAnswer: BufferedReader + readLine() in a loop — processes one line at a time without loading the whole file
questions.explanationHtml: For large files, you must avoid loading everything into memory at once. BufferedReader.readLine() reads one line at a time from a buffered stream, keeping memory usage constant regardless of file size. Files.lines() (a lazy Stream) is another good modern option. readAllLines() and readString() load the full file into memory.
